data.title: The Batman 2: Matt Reeves Officially Reveals Robert Pattinson’s New Look on Batman Day
data.incipit: The annual Bat day is here, and we have a new sneak peek of The Batman 2. Matt Reeves, who is helming the sequel, has shared a new look from the film ahead of its 2028 release. This year’s September 19, which...
data.body: The annual Bat day is here, and we have a new sneak peek of The Batman 2 . Matt Reeves, who is helming the sequel, has shared a new look from the film ahead of its 2028 release. This year’s September 19, which is celebrated as Batman Day, is significant, as the Robert Pattinson sequel is currently being filmed. Taking to X, Reeves shared a single photo showing a silhouette of the Dark Knight. The moody, cinematic shot does not reveal much. However, it sure adds to the existing excitement to see Pattinson’s Batman back on screen. “Happy Batman Day to everyone from London ,” Reeves wrote in the caption of the photo. Have a look at it here: Reeves is not the only DC director who celebrated Batman Day. Zack Snyder, who directed Batman v Superman and Justice League, shared a photo of Ben Affleck’s Batman, marking the day. James Gunn posted a Sam Kieth artwork from the Batman: Ghost s comic. Gunn is currently filming a Superman sequel with David Corenswet. Robert Pattinson’s Batman Returns With Updated Suit in Matt Reeves’ Sequel Robert Pattinson as Batman | Credit: Warner Bros. Pictures The Batman 2 will feature a more updated Batsuit for Robert Pattinson’s Dark Knight. In July 2026, when Matt Reeves first shared the camera test, it confirmed that the suit is not identical to its 2022 version. A fan also pointed out that the cowl now has longer ears. Reeves himself reposted the observation and confirmed, “You are not crazy.” Screenrant noted that there is some extra protection to the Batsuit, which is a chin guard that was spotted in the test footage. The outlet also claimed that the collars looked higher from the angles available for the suit. French publication Première examined some production photos, identifying a slight modification of the armor plates around the abdomen and torso. However, most of these remain speculations, except the ears of Batman’s cowl, which Reeves himself confirmed. The Batman 2 Picks Up After Gotham Flood Robert Pattinson in The Batman 2 Camera Test Footage | Credit: Warner Bros. Pictures Most of the plot for The Batman 2 is being kept under wraps. The available loglines (via Rotten Tomatoes) reveal that the sequel is set against the backdrop of the winter after the Gotham flood that engulfed the city at the end of the first film. Matt Reeves has revealed that the sequel will go beyond the aftermath of the disaster. He pointed out (via Variety ) that while the first film starring Pattinson is mostly focused on Batman, the sequel will explore more of the man behind the mask, Bruce Wayne. He noted that he “ never wanted to lose ” Pattinson “ at the center of” the origin stories. “ That is really what we set our aim on, ” Reeves added. The core trio of Robert Pattinson, Jeffrey Wright, and Andy Serkis will be returning in the sequel, along with Colin Farrell, Jayme Lawson, and Gil Perez-Abraham. The new casting roster includes Scarlett Johansson, Sebastian Stan, Charles Dance, and Sebastian Koch. The Batman 2 is now set for a February 18, 2028 theatrical release. What did you notice in the new look shared by Matt Reeves? Tell us in the comments.

data.title: Sure, it has ‘Star Wars,’ but the Lucas Museum’s free library and gardens are just as stellar
data.incipit: NewsTwo of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art’s most unique and transportive spaces don’t require a paid admission ticket.Written by Michael JulianoNational Things to Do Editor, U.S.Saturday September 19...
data.body: News Two of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art’s most unique and transportive spaces don’t require a paid admission ticket. Written by Michael Juliano National Things to Do Editor, U.S. Saturday September 19 2026 Share Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out | Library at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art You’ve probably already seen footage of the Star Wars props, the Van Gogh–inspired Pikachu and the striking spaceship-like architecture. But the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art’s most unique assets actually might be outside of the galleries—and, after it officially debuts on September 22, open to visitors for free, no museum ticket required. George Lucas has referred to his eponymous institution as a temple to the people’s art, where a self-portrait of Frida Kahlo, an oil painting of dogs playing poker and a screen-used Batman suit make unexpected neighbors. But that for-the-people perspective also— especially —extends to the entrancing gardens surrounding the building, as well as the open-to-the-public library . “I love that if you walk into our parks and gardens, you feel different,” says Lucas Museum CEO Tracey Bates. “You do feel like you’ve been transported somewhere else, which is the joy of storytelling—which is what the museum is all about.” Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out Lucas Museum of Narrative Art Whether you enter down the street from the Metro station on Vermont Avenue, across from the Natural History Museum and Coliseum at Bill Robertson Lane or into the middle of the Exposition Park –adjacent campus via the parking garage, you’ll find yourself in a mix of open grassy spaces and meandering walking paths. (Access here is completely separate from the museum galleries, which cost $25 for adults and nothing for kids 17 and under.) Dense clusters of native flora that’ve been maturing off-site for the past six years add much-needed greenery to what was once a parking lot. The cloud-shaped profile of the museum building, designed by Ma Yansong of MAD Architects, seems to float above the multi-tiered gardens. Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out Sculpture of Leia strangling Jabba the Hutt at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out Lucas Museum of Narrative Art And then there’s the bronze statue of Jabba the Hutt—being strangled by a shackle-wielding Leia. And Padmé fighting off a pillar-climbing nexu à la Attack of the Clones . Or a fountain topped with Yoda and his post-Disney-acquisition counterpart, Grogu. Star Wars may only represent 7% of the museum’s displays, but it’s well represented in the gardens. It’s not the only art on display, though: You’ll also find, among other pieces, sculptures of Rosie the Riveter, King Kong stop-motion animator Willis O’Brien and Terracotta Daughters , artist Prune Nourry’s response to China’s famous Terracotta Army. The free-to-visit park space, designed by Mia Lehrer and the team at Studio-MLA, also boasts a shallow amphitheater along its southern end. Though the full slate of programming is still to come, Bates expects that once a month on either Friday or Saturday (when the museum is open until 9pm), there’ll be a relatively large activation in the amphitheater (either for free or via accessibly priced tickets). Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out Lucas Museum of Narrative Art Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out Yoda and Grogu sculpture at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art But you don’t need a formal event to unwind in the garden: Bates invites people to come on their way home from school, before an LAFC match, to sit down and sketch, or for a meal at a picnic table after a visit to the California Science Center . “We want it to become part of their daily lives almost,” she says. “I just want people to feel safe, relaxed, and I’d love to inspire creativity here because that’s what George would want.” Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out Library at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art Speaking of creativity, the library here just might be the most imaginative space in the entire campus. Research libraries may typically give off a stuffy, studious air, but that’s certainly not the case at the Lucas Museum’s library, where light streams through the building’s spaceship-like shell and into a warm, Arts and Crafts–style sitting area with three floors of shelves carrying art books on everything from paleoart to Renaissance warfare to rock & roll posters. It’s an all-encompassing collection that library director Joan Jocson-Singh hopes will draw in all walks of visitors—and the free admission is certainly a strong incentive too. “The fact that we’re open to the community and that you don’t need to pay for a museum ticket really, I think, dismantles the notion that libraries are for a specific type of person,” she says. You’re welcome to peruse any of the books on the first-floor shelves and sit and linger as you read through them. (The library opens the same time as the museum and closes an hour earlier; just mention you’re headed there at the security checkpoint, look for the Naboo starfighter in the main plaza’s south building and then head up to the circulation desk.) Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out Lucas Museum of Narrative Art The collection started when the museum’s curators began researching some of the works that would ultimately go on display in the main galleries; these first-floor shelves mirror those themes, with books on comics, illustration and graphic arts, among other topics, and everything from Norman Rockwell to Dungeons & Dragons to the Separate Cinema Archive of early Black filmmaking. Spot any books with their covers facing out and they’re likely some of Jocson-Singh’s favorites, whether that’s a primer on Hollywood portrait photographers, a collection of He-Man illustrations or a celebration of Babar. And over on the tables, you’ll spot what she refers to as, well, table books: heavy, oversized Taschen editions that are typically kept behind a shop counter, but here they’re out in the open with X-Men comics, Donald Duck drawings or the sci-fi and fantasy works of Frank Frazetta. “Some of these books are out of print and rare,” Jocson-Singh says. “But it also gives you insight into our founders [George Lucas and Mellody Hobson]; you’re learning about the art that’s in the galleries that may not have titles that circulate widely, and it’s pretty unique because this museum is legitimizing and, what I like to say, academicizing art that hasn’t had a home before.” Photograph: Michael Juliano for Time Out Library at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art Though the mezzanine and third-floor shelves are off limits to the public, they’re filled with fascinating collections for researchers: titles about military history, vehicles, the occult, adventuring and Americana gifted straight from Lucas and Hobson’s personal collection at Skywalker Ranch (the museum shelves are even styled as an homage to that private library), as well as volumes on major art movements like modernism, cubism and Canadian landscape art that have been donated by Steve Martin. (Some museum-loving Angelenos may remember that the comedy icon curated an exhibition on that latter topic at the Hammer Museum about a decade ago.) All of the books in the library are non-circulating (so you can’t take them out of the room), and once you’re done reading, don’t bother trying to place them back on the shelves yourself: A bright orange book trolley with a photo of Yoda reminds you, “Reshelve, do not. Leave books here, you must!” You can expect to find a full catalog to browse on the museum’s website following the September 22 opening. For Jocson-Singh, that day is likely to be a pretty monumental moment. “The first time we started doing previews and had people in the space... seeing children come in and light up,” she says. “To see adults come in here and look at books that they had such invested interest in that you typically don’t see in a museum library just felt so rewarding.” Been there, done that?
